notes.front: What is a series wound generator?
notes.back: A DC generator whose field winding is connected in series with the external circuit, so all load current passes through the field.
notes.explanation: Its voltage rises as load rises, so the handbook says aircraft generators use shunt or compound field connections instead.
notes.example: Like a shunt wound generator in having one field winding, but that winding sits in the load path instead of across it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Series Wound DC Generators”, PDF page 171
notes.evidence: The series generator contains a field winding connected in series with the external circuit.

notes.front: What is a shunt wound generator?
notes.back: A DC generator whose field winding is connected in parallel (shunt) with the external circuit; also called a parallel generator.
notes.explanation: In electrical terms shunt means parallel; with the compound wound type, it is one of the two field connections aircraft generators use.
notes.example: Like a series wound generator in having one field winding, but that winding is connected across the output rather than in the load path.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Parallel (Shunt) Wound DC Generators”, PDF page 171
notes.evidence: A generator having a field winding connected in parallel with the external circuit is called a shunt generator. [Figure 4-22] It should be noted that, in electrical terms, shunt means parallel.

notes.front: What is a compound wound generator?
notes.back: A DC generator with two field windings: one in series and one in parallel with the load.
notes.explanation: Combining the two windings lets it take advantage of both the series and the parallel characteristics.
notes.example: Like a shunt wound generator with a series winding added, so it carries both kinds of field at once.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Compound Wound DC Generators”, PDF page 172
notes.evidence: A compound wound generator employs two field windings one in series and another in parallel with the load. [Figure 4-23] This arrangement takes advantage of both the series and parallel characteristics described earlier.

notes.front: What is a reverse current relay?
notes.back: The unit of a three-unit regulator that stops current leaving the battery and feeding the generator.
notes.explanation: The General deck calls it the reverse current cut-out relay; current flowing from the battery into the generator would discharge the battery, the opposite of normal operation.
notes.example: Like a one-way valve in a fuel line, but for current between the battery and the generator.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Reverse-Current Relay”, PDF page 452
notes.evidence: The third unit of a three-unit regulator is used to prevent current from leaving the battery and feeding the generator. This type of current flow would discharge the battery and is opposite of normal operation.

notes.front: What does overvoltage protection in a generator control system do?
notes.back: It compares sampled voltage with a reference voltage and opens the relay that controls field excitation current.
notes.explanation: Opening that relay removes the field excitation, and the handbook notes the feature is typically found on more complex generator control systems.
notes.example: Like a cut-out on a pressure cooker, but it trips the generator field instead of venting steam.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Overvoltage Protection”, PDF page 450
notes.evidence: The overvoltage protection system compares the sampled voltage to a reference voltage. The overvoltage protection circuit is used to open the relay that controls the field excitation current. It is typically found on more complex generator control systems.

notes.front: What is a DC alternator?
notes.back: An alternator whose three-phase AC armature output is rectified to DC for the aircraft's DC loads.
notes.explanation: The armature naturally produces AC, which is not compatible with typical DC loads, so it must be rectified.
notes.example: Like a DC generator in powering a DC bus, but it makes AC internally and changes it to DC with diodes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “DC Alternators & Controls”, PDF page 454
notes.evidence: Since the three-phase voltage produced by the alternators armature is AC, it is not compatible with typical DC electrical loads and must be rectified (changed to DC).

notes.front: What does an alternator voltage regulator control, and how?
notes.back: Alternator output, by adjusting the alternator's field current, just as a DC generator regulator does.
notes.explanation: The handbook says regulators for DC alternators work on the same general concept as those for DC generators.
notes.example: Like a generator's voltage regulator, but modern ones are solid-state units with no moving parts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Alternator Voltage Regulators”, PDF page 455
notes.evidence: Voltage regulators for DC alternators are similar to those found on DC generators. The general concepts are the same in that adjusting alternator field current controls alternator output.

notes.front: What is an AC alternator, and which aircraft use one?
notes.back: An engine-driven machine producing three-phase AC; found only on aircraft that use a large amount of electrical power.
notes.explanation: Virtually all transport category aircraft have one driven by each engine.
notes.example: Like a DC alternator inside, but its three-phase output goes to the buses without being rectified.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “AC Alternators”, PDF page 456
notes.evidence: AC alternators are found only on aircraft that use a large amount of electrical power. Virtually all transport category aircraft, such as the Boeing 757 or the Airbus A-380, employ one AC alternator driven by each engine.

notes.front: What is an integrated drive generator (IDG)?
notes.back: A constant speed drive and an AC alternator contained in one unit.
notes.explanation: The CSD can be a separate unit or sit inside the alternator housing; the combined assembly is what the IDG name describes.
notes.example: Like a separate CSD bolted to an alternator, but both are packed into a single housing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Alternator Drive”, PDF page 459
notes.evidence: The CSD can be an independent unit or mounted within the alternator housing. When the CSD and the alternator are contained within one unit, the assembly is known as an integrated drive generator (IDG).

notes.front: What must every AC alternator control unit regulate?
notes.back: Both voltage and frequency.
notes.explanation: Unlike DC systems, AC systems must also keep output frequency within limits, so the control units handle both.
notes.example: Like a DC voltage regulator, but it must also hold the output near 400 Hz.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “AC Alternators Control Systems”, PDF page 460
notes.evidence: All AC alternator control units contain circuitry that regulates both voltage and frequency.

notes.front: What is paralleling?
notes.back: Equalising the outputs of two or more alternators or generators so they share the electrical load equally.
notes.explanation: On a twin, both machines feed the same load, and it becomes vital that each carries an equal share.
notes.example: Like two horses in harness pulling the same cart, but a control circuit keeps either from doing more than half the work.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Paralleling Alternators or Generators”, PDF page 472
notes.evidence: Since two alternators (or generators) are used on twin engine aircraft, it becomes vital to ensure both alternators share the electrical load equally. This process of equalizing alternator outputs is often called paralleling.

notes.front: What is a starter-generator?
notes.back: One unit that starts a gas turbine engine and then, with its circuitry shifted, works as the generator.
notes.explanation: It is used on many smaller gas-turbine engines, where one component does both jobs.
notes.example: Like a separate starter and generator on the same gearbox, but combined into one machine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Glossary: Starter-generator”, PDF page 484
notes.evidence: A single-component starter and generator used on many smaller gas-turbine engines. It is used to start the engine, and when the engine is running, its circuitry is shifted so that it acts as a generator.

notes.front: Why does the handbook stress care with powerplant wiring?
notes.back: Improperly or carelessly installed or maintained wiring can be a source of both immediate and potential danger.
notes.explanation: The handbook ties aircraft performance closely to the continuing reliability of electrical systems.
notes.example: Like a fuel line in needing correct routing and support, but a chafed wire can fail invisibly until it shorts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Powerplant Electrical Systems”, PDF page 206
notes.evidence: The satisfactory performance of any modern aircraft depends to a great degree on the continuing reliability of electrical systems and subsystems. Improperly or carelessly installed or maintained wiring can be a source of both immediate and potential danger.

notes.front: What is the American Wire Gauge (AWG)?
notes.back: The standard to which wire sizes are made; the larger the gauge number, the smaller the wire diameter.
notes.explanation: Gauge numbers let wires be compared by diameter; the handbook notes the diameters shrink as numbers rise.
notes.example: Like shoe sizes in giving each size a number, but reversed: a No. 20 wire is thinner than a No. 10.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Wire Size”, PDF page 207
notes.evidence: Wire is manufactured in sizes according to a standard known as the American wire gauge (AWG). The wire diameters become smaller as the gauge numbers become larger.

notes.front: What are the two fundamental properties of wire insulation materials?
notes.back: Insulation resistance and dielectric strength.
notes.explanation: The handbook stresses that these are entirely different and distinct properties.
notes.example: Like a hose wall that must both not seep and not burst: seepage is insulation resistance, bursting pressure is dielectric strength.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Conductor Insulation”, PDF page 211
notes.evidence: Two fundamental properties of insulation materials (e.g., rubber, glass, asbestos, and plastic) are insulation resistance and dielectric strength. These are entirely different and distinct properties.

notes.front: What is lacing, as applied to wire bundles?
notes.back: Securing a wire group or bundle with one continuous cord forming loops at regular intervals.
notes.explanation: The handbook separates it from tying, which uses individual pieces of cord at intervals.
notes.example: Like lacing a boot with one long lace, but the loops wrap round a bundle of wires.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Lacing & Tying Wire Bundles”, PDF page 217
notes.evidence: Lacing is the securing together of a group or bundle of wires by a continuous piece of cord forming loops at regular intervals around the group or bundle.

notes.front: What is a solderless terminal lug for?
notes.back: Terminating a wire so it can be easily connected to and disconnected from terminal blocks, bus bars or other equipment.
notes.explanation: The lug gives an easy, efficient connection that can also be undone.
notes.example: Like a ring on the end of a battery cable, but crimped onto the wire instead of soldered.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Solderless Terminals & Splices”, PDF page 220
notes.evidence: Electric wires are terminated with solderless terminal lugs to permit easy and efficient connection to and disconnection from terminal blocks, bus bars, or other electrical equipment.

notes.front: What is bonding?
notes.back: Electrically connecting two or more conducting objects that are not otherwise connected adequately.
notes.explanation: The handbook defines it beside grounding, which connects an object to primary structure for return of current.
notes.example: Like grounding in using a conductor between metal parts, but its aim is to join the parts to each other, not to provide a return path.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Bonding & Grounding”, PDF page 224
notes.evidence: Bonding is the electrical connecting of two or more conducting objects not otherwise connected adequately.

notes.front: What is a bonding jumper usually made of?
notes.back: Aluminium alloy in most cases; copper jumpers may bond parts of stainless steel, cadmium-plated steel, copper, brass or bronze.
notes.explanation: Aluminium alloy is the recommended default; copper is used for the listed metals.
notes.example: Like a short earth strap across a hinge, but chosen in a metal that suits the parts it joins.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Bonding & Grounding”, PDF page 224
notes.evidence: Aluminum alloy jumpers are recommended for most cases; however, copper jumpers can be used to bond together parts made of stainless steel, cadmium-plated steel, copper, brass, or bronze.

notes.front: What is an AN or MS connector?
notes.back: An Army/Navy or Military Standard electrical connector made of two parts: a plug assembly and a receptacle assembly.
notes.explanation: Such connectors simplify most firewall disconnections of electrical conduit and cable.
notes.example: Like a household plug and socket, but with a threaded coupling that can be safety wired.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Removal of Reciprocating Engines: disconnecting electrical leads”, PDF page 334
notes.evidence: Most firewall disconnections of electrical conduit and cable are simplified by use of (Army/Navy) AN or (Military Standard) MS connectors. Each connector consists of two parts: a plug assembly and a receptacle assembly.

notes.front: What is conduit used for in aircraft wiring?
notes.back: Mechanical protection of wires and cables; it comes in metallic and nonmetallic, rigid and flexible forms.
notes.explanation: It is available in metallic or nonmetallic, rigid or flexible form.
notes.example: Like a garden hose sleeve over a cable, but specified with room to spare for later circuits.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Conduit”, PDF page 228
notes.evidence: Conduit is used in aircraft installations for the mechanical protection of wires and cables. It is available in metallic and nonmetallic materials and in both rigid and flexible form.

notes.front: What is a SWAMP (severe wind and moisture problem) area?
notes.back: An exterior area with a harsh environment, usually wheel wells, near wing flaps, wing folds and pylons.
notes.explanation: Wires there often need an exterior jacket to protect them from the environment.
notes.example: Like the underside of a car wheel arch: wet, dirty and flexing, so wiring there needs extra protection.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Areas Designated as Severe Wind & Moisture Problem (SWAMP)”, PDF page 484
notes.evidence: SWAMP areas differ from aircraft to aircraft but are usually wheel wells, near wing flaps, wing folds, pylons, and other exterior areas that may have a harsh environment. Wires in these areas have often an exterior jacket to protect them from the environment.

notes.front: What are the three types of DC generator?
notes.back: Series wound, shunt (parallel) wound and compound (series-parallel) wound.
notes.explanation: The type is set by how the armature and field circuits connect with respect to the external circuit.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Types of DC Generators”, PDF page 171
notes.evidence: There are three types of DC generators: series wound, parallel (shunt) wound, and series-parallel (compound) wound. The appropriate generator is determined by the connections to the armature and field circuits with respect to the external circuit.

notes.front: What happens if a generator of the wrong rotation direction is fitted?
notes.back: The polarity of the output voltage is reversed.
notes.explanation: Rotation is stated as clockwise or counterclockwise viewed from the driven end, and may be stamped on the data plate.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Generator Ratings”, PDF page 172
notes.evidence: The rotation of generators is termed either clockwise or counterclockwise, as viewed from the driven end. The direction of rotation may also be stamped on the data plate. It is important that a generator with the correct rotation be used; otherwise, the polarity of the output voltage is reversed.

notes.front: Why must emery cloth never be used to seat brushes or smooth a commutator?
notes.back: It contains conductive material that causes arcing between brushes and commutator bars.
notes.explanation: The handbook prohibits it "under no circumstances" for this reason.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Generator Maintenance”, PDF page 449
notes.evidence: Under no circumstances should emery cloth or similar abrasives be used for seating brushes (or smoothing commutators), since they contain conductive materials that cause arcing between brushes and commutator bars.

notes.front: What do excessive and too little brush spring pressure each cause?
notes.back: Excessive: rapid brush wear. Too little: bouncing brushes with burned and pitted surfaces.
notes.explanation: The manufacturer's pressure is checked with a spring scale graduated in ounces.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Generator Maintenance”, PDF page 449
notes.evidence: Excessive pressure causes rapid wear of brushes. Too little pressure, however, allows bouncing of the brushes, resulting in burned and pitted surfaces. The pressure recommended by the manufacturer should be checked by the use of a spring scale graduated in ounces.

notes.front: An engine data plate lists a replacement DC generator whose output must stay nearly steady as cabin loads switch on and off. Which winding arrangement best fits?
notes.choices:
A) Series wound
B) Shunt wound with no regulator
C) Compound wound
D) A permanent magnet with no field winding
notes.back: C) Compound wound
notes.choicesExplained: A: its voltage rises and falls with load, and it is never used as an aeroplane generator. B: its voltage falls as load rises. D: none of the three DC generator types described works this way.
notes.explanation: A compound wound generator's output is relatively constant even with changes in load.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Compound Wound DC Generators”, PDF page 172
notes.evidence: The output of a compound wound generator is relatively constant, even with changes in the load.

notes.front: A mechanic is choosing a DC generator for an aircraft with a 24-volt battery. Which rating fits?
notes.choices:
A) 24 volts
B) 28 volts
C) 12 volts
D) 14 volts
notes.back: B) 28 volts
notes.choicesExplained: A: the generator must be slightly higher than the battery voltage. C: that is below even a 12-volt system's generator rating. D: that suits a 12-volt battery.
notes.explanation: The handbook requires generator output slightly higher than battery voltage.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Generator Ratings”, PDF page 172
notes.evidence: Batteries are either 12 or 24 volts when fully charged. The generator selected must have a voltage output slightly higher than the battery voltage. Hence, the 14- or 28-volt rating is required for aircraft DC generators.

notes.front: After a generator change, the new unit's output polarity is found reversed. What is the most likely cause?
notes.choices:
A) The brushes were seated with 000 sandpaper
B) A generator with the wrong direction of rotation was fitted
C) The coming-in speed is about 1,500 rpm
D) The generator is rated in amperes
notes.back: B) A generator with the wrong direction of rotation was fitted
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is the recommended way to seat brushes. C: a speed figure has nothing to do with which way the output polarity runs. D: every generator’s power output is given that way.
notes.explanation: The handbook warns that fitting a generator of the wrong rotation reverses the output polarity.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Generator Ratings”, PDF page 172
notes.evidence: It is important that a generator with the correct rotation be used; otherwise, the polarity of the output voltage is reversed.

notes.front: On inspection, a generator's brushes show burned and pitted surfaces. Which fault does this point to?
notes.choices:
A) Too little brush spring pressure
B) Brushes seated with fine sandpaper
C) Excessive brush spring pressure
D) Oil in the generator
notes.back: A) Too little brush spring pressure
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is the approved seating method. C: that causes rapid brush wear instead. D: that sends you to the engine oil seals, not the brush springs.
notes.explanation: Too little pressure lets the brushes bounce, which burns and pits them.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “DC Generator Maintenance”, PDF page 173
notes.evidence: Too little pressure, however, allows bouncing of the brushes, resulting in burned and pitted surfaces.

notes.front: What do the three relays of a three-unit regulator do?
notes.back: Regulate voltage, limit current and prevent reverse current flow.
notes.explanation: Each relay monitors generator output and opens or closes its points as the system needs.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Three-Unit Regulators”, PDF page 452
notes.evidence: The three relays found on this regulator are used to regulate voltage, limit current, and prevent reverse current flow.

notes.front: What does a reverse current relay do when generator output is lost?
notes.back: Its contact points open, disconnecting the generator from the aircraft electrical system.
notes.explanation: Magnetism in the relay is lost with no output, and the open points stop reverse flow from the bus to the generator.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Reverse-Current Relay”, PDF page 453
notes.evidence: If there is no generator output due to a system failure, the contact points open because magnetism in the relay is lost. With the contact points open, the generator is automatically disconnected from the aircraft electrical system, which prevents reverse flow from the load bus to the generator.

notes.front: On a twin, one generator fails and the other starts supplying nearly all the load and too much current. Which control function acts?
notes.choices:
A) Overexcitation protection
B) Reverse current sensing
C) Differential voltage
D) Voltage regulation alone
notes.back: A) Overexcitation protection
notes.choicesExplained: B: it disconnects a generator that draws current, not one supplying too much. C: it checks voltages before a generator connects to the bus. D: the handbook names a separate function for this condition.
notes.explanation: The overexcited generator must be brought back within limits, or damage occurs.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Overexcitation Protection”, PDF page 450
notes.evidence: If this condition is sensed, the overexcited generator must be brought back within limits, or damage occurs.

notes.front: A running engine's generator drive shaft shears in flight. Which unit keeps the battery from discharging back into the dead generator?
notes.choices:
A) The field rheostat
B) The current limiter
C) The voltage regulator relay
D) The reverse current relay
notes.back: D) The reverse current relay
notes.choicesExplained: A: it only varies field resistance. B: it limits generator output current; it does not stop flow into the generator. C: it controls field current to hold voltage.
notes.explanation: With no output, the relay loses magnetism and its points open, cutting the generator off the bus.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Reverse-Current Relay”, PDF page 452
notes.evidence: The third unit of a three-unit regulator is used to prevent current from leaving the battery and feeding the generator. This type of current flow would discharge the battery and is opposite of normal operation.

notes.front: A generator control system senses output voltage well above its reference. What does the overvoltage circuit open?
notes.choices:
A) The main battery switch
B) The relay that controls the field excitation current
C) The engine ignition circuit
D) The current limiter points
notes.back: B) The relay that controls the field excitation current
notes.choicesExplained: A: the overvoltage circuit acts on field excitation, not the battery. C: generator protection does not act on ignition. D: those open on extreme current, not overvoltage.
notes.explanation: The overvoltage circuit acts by opening the field excitation relay after comparing sampled and reference voltage.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Overvoltage Protection”, PDF page 450
notes.evidence: The overvoltage protection circuit is used to open the relay that controls the field excitation current.

notes.front: How do DC alternators compare with DC generators in weight and efficiency?
notes.back: They are generally lighter and more efficient.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that they are found on modern, light, piston-engine aircraft.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “DC Alternators & Controls”, PDF page 453
notes.evidence: In general, DC alternators are lighter and more efficient than DC generators. DC alternators and their related controls are found on modern, light, piston-engine aircraft.

notes.front: Besides regulation, what protection may a solid-state alternator regulator provide?
notes.back: Any two: over- or under-voltage protection, overcurrent protection, or monitoring for internal defects such as a defective diode.
notes.explanation: Solid-state regulators typically add protection circuitry not found in vibrating-type regulators.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Alternator Voltage Regulators”, PDF page 455
notes.evidence: Protection may include over- or under-voltage protection, overcurrent protection, as well as monitoring the alternator for internal defects, such as a defective diode.

notes.front: A light aircraft owner wants the DC alternator regulator that needs least maintenance and regulates most accurately. Which type fits?
notes.choices:
A) A vibrating-relay regulator
B) A carbon pile regulator
C) A solid-state regulator
D) A manual field rheostat
notes.back: C) A solid-state regulator
notes.choicesExplained: A: its moving points make it less reliable and less accurate. B: it needs regular maintenance and has mostly been replaced. D: a hand-set rheostat only varies field resistance; it does not follow the load by itself.
notes.explanation: Solid-state units have no moving parts and are generally considered more reliable with better regulation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Alternator Voltage Regulators”, PDF page 455
notes.evidence: These units contain no moving parts and are generally considered to be more reliable and provide better system regulation than vibrating-type regulators.

notes.front: A light aircraft's DC alternator gives an output with heavy AC content on the bus. Which part most likely failed?
notes.choices:
A) The constant speed drive
B) A diode in the rectifier assembly
C) The exciter permanent magnet
D) The paralleling coil
notes.back: B) A diode in the rectifier assembly
notes.choicesExplained: A: light DC alternators are belt or gear driven without one. C: that belongs to a brushless AC alternator. D: it balances two alternators; it does not rectify.
notes.explanation: The armature makes three-phase AC, and the diodes change it to DC for the loads.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “DC Alternators & Controls”, PDF page 454
notes.evidence: Therefore, the armature output current is sent through a rectifier assembly that changes the three-phase AC to DC.

notes.front: How far apart are the three voltages of an AC alternator?
notes.explanation: Each revolution produces three separate voltages, and the AC alternator does not rectify them.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “AC Alternators”, PDF page 456
notes.evidence: AC alternators produce a three-phase AC output. For each revolution of the alternator, the unit produces three separate voltages. The sine waves for these voltages are separated by 120°.

notes.front: Why is the modern AC alternator called brushless?
notes.back: It has no brushes or slip rings; energy reaches the rotor by magnetic flux and induction.
notes.explanation: The design is extremely reliable and needs very little maintenance.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “AC Alternators”, PDF page 456
notes.evidence: The modern AC alternator does not utilize brushes or slip rings and is often referred to as a brushless AC alternator. This brushless design is extremely reliable and requires very little maintenance.

notes.front: What frequency should aircraft AC alternators produce, and what deviation upsets the systems?
notes.back: About 400 Hz; straying more than 10 percent stops the electrical systems operating correctly.
notes.explanation: So every AC alternator must turn at a specific rpm to keep frequency within limits.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Alternator Drive”, PDF page 459
notes.evidence: Aircraft AC alternators should produce a frequency of approximately 400 Hz. If the frequency strays more than 10 percent from this value, the electrical systems do not operate correctly.

notes.front: How often is the oil level in an oil-cooled alternator and constant speed drive checked?
notes.back: Routinely: the handbook calls the level critical and says it is typically checked on a routine basis.
notes.explanation: The same oil supplied from the drive circulates through the alternator to cool it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Alternator Drive”, PDF page 459
notes.evidence: ports make oil flow between the constant speed drive and the generator possible. This oil level is critical and typically checked on a routine basis.

notes.front: Why do alternators driven by an auxiliary power unit usually need no constant speed drive?
notes.back: The APU runs at a constant rpm, so the directly driven alternator already gives 400 Hz.
notes.explanation: The APU speed control adjusts engine rpm if the frequency drifts from 400 Hz.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Alternator Drive”, PDF page 459
notes.evidence: On many aircraft, the auxiliary power unit operates at a constant rpm. AC alternators driven by these APUs are typically driven directly by the engine, and there is no CSD required.

notes.front: On a transport aircraft, an engine's AC alternator frequency drifts as the pilot changes thrust. Which unit should hold it steady?
notes.choices:
A) The constant speed drive
B) The reverse current relay
C) The pilot exciter
D) The rectifier assembly
notes.back: A) The constant speed drive
notes.choicesExplained: B: it belongs to DC generator regulators. C: it feeds the voltage regulation circuit, not the drive speed. D: an AC alternator does not rectify its output.
notes.explanation: The drive keeps alternator speed, and so frequency, constant from just above idle to maximum rpm.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Alternator Drive”, PDF page 459
notes.evidence: The constant-speed drive enables the alternator to produce the same frequency at slightly above engine idle rpm as it does at maximum engine rpm.

notes.front: How closely must a twin's paralleling system match the two power producers' voltage?
notes.back: Within a few tenths of a volt.
notes.explanation: Alternators on the same bus at the same voltage share the load equally.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Paralleling Alternators or Generators”, PDF page 472
notes.evidence: the paralleling systems must ensure both power producers maintain system voltage within a few tenths of a volt.

notes.front: When does a paralleling relay open?
notes.back: Automatically whenever the output of either alternator or generator drops to zero.
notes.explanation: It shuts off the paralleling current that normally keeps the machines sharing load equally.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Glossary: Paralleling relay”, PDF page 1017
notes.evidence: The relay opens automatically to shut off the flow of paralleling current any time the output of either alternator or generator drops to zero.

notes.front: On a twin at cruise, the left alternator is at 28.0 volts and the right at 26.0 volts on a shared bus. What does this show?
notes.choices:
A) Normal operation, as both are between 26 and 28 volts
B) Paralleling is not working: voltages should be within a few tenths of a volt
C) Reverse current, so the right alternator must be failed
D) An overvoltage condition on the left
notes.back: B) Paralleling is not working: voltages should be within a few tenths of a volt
notes.choicesExplained: A: a two-volt gap is far more than a few tenths. C: a lower voltage alone does not show current flowing into it. D: 28 volts is within the twin's normal range.
notes.explanation: Unequal voltages mean unequal load sharing, which paralleling exists to prevent.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Paralleling Alternators or Generators”, PDF page 472
notes.evidence: For most twin-engine aircraft, the voltage would be between 26.5-volt and 28-volt DC with the alternators operating.

notes.front: In a starter-generator, which field does the control unit energise for starting, and which for generating?
notes.back: Series field for starting; parallel field for generating, with the series field disconnected.
notes.explanation: Energising the series field makes the unit act as a motor.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Generator Controls for High-Output Generators”, PDF page 450
notes.evidence: During the start function, the GCU must energize the series field and the armature causes the unit to act like a motor. During the generating mode, the GCU must disconnect the series field, energize the parallel field

notes.front: A turboprop needs one engine-mounted electrical unit that turns the engine for start and then supplies bus power. Which unit is it?
notes.choices:
A) An integrated drive generator
B) A DC alternator with a rectifier
C) A starter-generator
D) A series wound generator
notes.back: C) A starter-generator
notes.choicesExplained: A: it combines a constant speed drive with an AC alternator and does not start the engine. B: it generates only. D: it is never used as an aeroplane generator.
notes.explanation: The starter-generator starts the engine and, with its circuitry shifted, then acts as the generator.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Glossary: Starter-generator”, PDF page 484
notes.evidence: It is used to start the engine, and when the engine is running, its circuitry is shifted so that it acts as a generator.

notes.front: A mechanic has No. 12 and No. 16 wire on the bench. Which has the larger diameter?
notes.choices:
A) No. 16
B) Both are the same diameter
C) No. 12
D) It cannot be told from the numbers
notes.back: C) No. 12
notes.choicesExplained: A: larger gauge numbers mean smaller diameters. B: each gauge number is a different size. D: the gauge numbers compare diameters directly.
notes.explanation: On the American Wire Gauge, diameter shrinks as the number grows.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Wire Size”, PDF page 207
notes.evidence: The wire diameters become smaller as the gauge numbers become larger.

notes.front: Which wire-size factor is electrical energy converted into heat in the line?
notes.back: The allowable power loss.
notes.explanation: Larger conductors cut resistance and so this loss, but cost more and weigh more.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Factors Affecting the Selection of Wire Size”, PDF page 207
notes.evidence: One factor is the allowable power loss (PR loss) in the line. This loss represents electrical energy converted into heat. The use of large conductors reduces the resistance and therefore the PR loss.

notes.front: Which wire-size factor, if it varies widely, gives poor voltage regulation at the load?
notes.back: The permissible voltage drop in the line.
notes.explanation: Load changes vary line current and so the drop; a compromise keeps variation tolerable without excessive weight.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Factors Affecting the Selection of Wire Size”, PDF page 209
notes.evidence: A wide variation in the IR drop in the line causes poor voltage regulation at the load.

notes.front: Which wire-size factor limits current so the conductor's heat does not damage its insulation?
notes.back: The current carrying ability of the conductor.
notes.explanation: Insulation keeps the heat in, so current must be kept low enough to protect it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Factors Affecting the Selection of Wire Size”, PDF page 209
notes.evidence: Thus, to protect the insulation from too much heat, the current through the conductor must be maintained

notes.front: A wire run in a hot engine area is sized correctly for voltage drop, yet its insulation keeps overheating. Which selection factor was not satisfied?
notes.choices:
A) Wire identification
B) Allowable power loss only
C) Permissible voltage drop
D) Current carrying ability, allowing for external heating
notes.back: D) Current carrying ability, allowing for external heating
notes.choicesExplained: A: marking has nothing to do with heating. B: the symptom is insulation heat, which the current-capacity factor addresses. C: the run already meets its drop limit.
notes.explanation: In hot locations external heat adds to conductor heating, so allowable current must be reduced.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Factors Affecting the Selection of Wire Size”, PDF page 209
notes.evidence: Allowance must be made for the influence of external heating on the allowable conductor current, and each case has its own specific limitations.

notes.front: What is the voltage drop limit in the main power cables from the generator or battery to the bus?
notes.back: 2 percent of the regulated voltage.
notes.explanation: It applies with the generator at rated current or the battery at a 5-minute discharge rate.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Voltage Drop in Aircraft Wire & Cable”, PDF page 209
notes.evidence: The voltage drop in the main power cables from the aircraft generation source or the battery to the bus should not exceed 2 percent of the regulated voltage when the generator is carrying rated current or the battery is being discharged at a 5-minute rate.

notes.front: What voltage drop is allowed in a 28-volt load circuit, for continuous and for intermittent operation?
notes.back: 1 volt continuous; 2 volts intermittent.
notes.explanation: The allowance scales with system voltage, and intermittent loads are allowed twice the continuous figure.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Voltage Drop in Aircraft Wire & Cable (Figure 4-85)”, PDF page 210
notes.evidence: Nominal System Voltage Continuous Operation Intermittent Operation 14 0.5 1 28 1 2 115 4 8 200 7 14

image.alt: Table of recommended maximum voltage drop in load circuits between bus and equipment: 14-volt system, 0.5 volt continuous and 1 volt intermittent; 28-volt system, 1 and 2; 115-volt system, 4 and 8; 200-volt system, 7 and 14.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from FAA-H-8083-32B, Figure 4-85

notes.front: What continuous voltage drop is allowed in a 14-volt load circuit?
notes.back: 0.5 volt.
notes.explanation: It is half the 28-volt figure; intermittent operation allows 1 volt.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Voltage Drop in Aircraft Wire & Cable (Figure 4-85)”, PDF page 210
notes.evidence: Allowable Voltage Drop Nominal System Voltage Continuous Operation Intermittent Operation 14 0.5 1

notes.front: A new 28-volt landing light circuit, used only intermittently, measures a 1.5-volt drop from bus to lamp. Is that within the recommended limit?
notes.choices:
A) Yes: 2 volts is allowed for intermittent operation
B) No: the limit is 0.5 volt
C) Yes: any drop under 4 volts is fine
D) No: only 1 volt is ever allowed at 28 volts
notes.back: A) Yes: 2 volts is allowed for intermittent operation
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is the 14-volt continuous figure. C: 4 volts is the 115-volt continuous figure. D: 1 volt is the continuous figure.
notes.explanation: The table gives 28-volt circuits 1 volt continuous and 2 volts intermittent.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Voltage Drop in Aircraft Wire & Cable (Figure 4-85)”, PDF page 210
notes.evidence: Nominal System Voltage Continuous Operation Intermittent Operation 14 0.5 1 28 1 2

notes.front: What are two things you must know to size a wire with the electrical wire chart?
notes.back: Any two of: wire length in feet, current in amperes, allowable voltage drop, continuous or intermittent current, conductor temperature.
notes.explanation: The chart is read from wire length and current for a given system voltage against its allowable drop.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 11, “11-68. Instructions for Use of Electrical Wire Chart”, PDF page 600
notes.evidence: (1) The wire length in feet. (2) The number of amperes of current to be carried. (3) The allowable voltage drop permitted. (4) The required continuous or intermittent current. (5) The estimated or measured conductor temperature.

notes.front: When the wire chart result falls between two gauge sizes, which do you choose?
notes.back: The next larger wire (the smaller gauge number).
notes.explanation: The larger size is the smallest that keeps the drop within the limit.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Voltage Drop in Aircraft Wire & Cable”, PDF page 211
notes.evidence: Since the indicated value is between two numbers, the larger size, No. 8, should be selected. This is the smallest size that should be used to avoid an excessive voltage drop.

notes.front: Using the continuous-flow chart, a new circuit's point lands between No. 14 and No. 12. Which wire should be installed?
notes.choices:
A) No. 12
B) No. 14
C) No. 16
D) Either, as both are close
notes.back: A) No. 12
notes.choicesExplained: B: it is the smaller wire and would exceed the voltage drop limit. C: it is smaller still. D: the rule is to take the larger size.
notes.explanation: Choose the next larger wire: the smaller gauge number.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, chapter 11, “11-68. Instructions for Use of Electrical Wire Chart”, PDF page 601
notes.evidence: Select the next larger size wire to the right, in this case No. 8. This is the smallest size wire that can be used without exceeding the voltage drop limit

notes.front: At what spacing do most manufacturers mark wires?
notes.back: At intervals of not more than 15 inches, and within 3 inches of each junction or terminating point.
notes.explanation: Markings tie each wire to its circuit and the wiring diagram, which aids testing and repair.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Identifying Wire & Cable”, PDF page 212
notes.evidence: Most manufacturers mark the wires at intervals of not more than 15 inches lengthwise and within 3 inches of each junction or terminating point.

notes.front: A replacement wire 40 inches long runs between two terminals. Which marking layout meets the usual practice?
notes.choices:
A) One mark in the middle only
B) Marks every 24 inches
C) Marks within 3 inches of each end and no more than 15 inches apart
D) No marks, as the wiring diagram is enough
notes.back: C) Marks within 3 inches of each end and no more than 15 inches apart
notes.choicesExplained: A: marks are needed near each terminating point. B: the interval is not more than 15 inches. D: marking relates the wire to the diagram.
notes.explanation: Most manufacturers mark at not more than 15-inch intervals and within 3 inches of each junction.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Identifying Wire & Cable”, PDF page 212
notes.evidence: Most manufacturers mark the wires at intervals of not more than 15 inches lengthwise and within 3 inches of each junction or terminating point.

notes.front: Which wires should not be grouped or bundled together?
notes.back: Electrically unprotected power wiring, and wiring to duplicate vital equipment.
notes.explanation: Unprotected wiring runs from generators to main bus points without fuses or breakers.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Wire Groups & Bundles”, PDF page 213
notes.evidence: Grouping or bundling certain wires, such as electrically unprotected power wiring and wiring to duplicate vital equipment, should be avoided.

notes.front: Between two clamps, a wire bundle deflects about 1 inch with normal hand force, and the bundle is not thin. What should be done?
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: 1 inch is normal
B) Remove all slack so the bundle is tight
C) Add a grommet
D) Reduce the slack to about ½ inch
notes.back: D) Reduce the slack to about ½ inch
notes.choicesExplained: A: slack between supports should normally not exceed ½ inch. B: some slack is needed near ends for maintenance and strain relief. C: grommets protect wires at holes, not slack.
notes.explanation: The normal limit is ½ inch between supports, with more only for thin bundles and widely spaced clamps.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Slack in Wiring Bundles”, PDF page 213
notes.evidence: Slack between supports should normally not exceed ½ inch.

notes.front: A bundle 0.5 inch in outside diameter must turn a corner in open structure, away from any terminal strip. What is its smallest acceptable bend radius?
notes.choices:
A) 3 inches
B) 1.5 inches
C) 0.5 inch
D) 5 inches
notes.back: D) 5 inches
notes.choicesExplained: A: six times diameter is not the general bundle rule. B: three times diameter applies only at supported terminal strips. C: that is just one diameter.
notes.explanation: Bundles bend no tighter than ten times outside diameter: 10 × 0.5 = 5 inches.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Bend Radii”, PDF page 214
notes.evidence: Bends in wire groups or bundles should not be less than ten times the outside diameter of the wire group or bundle.

notes.front: When must a grommet be fitted where wires pass through a hole?
notes.back: When the wires come closer than ¼ inch to the hole's edge.
notes.explanation: Contact with sharp edges damages insulation and can cause short circuits.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Protection Against Chafing”, PDF page 215
notes.evidence: If wires come closer than ¼ inch to the edge of the hole, a suitable grommet is used in the hole.

notes.front: A new wire bundle passes through a bulkhead hole with the wires about ⅛ inch from the hole edge. What is required?
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, as long as the bundle is laced
B) Wrap the wires in tape only
C) A suitable grommet in the hole, with a cable clamp supporting the bundle
D) Route the bundle through the lowest four inches of the fuselage instead
notes.back: C) A suitable grommet in the hole, with a cable clamp supporting the bundle
notes.choicesExplained: A: lacing does not stop chafing at the hole edge. B: the handbook calls for a grommet within ¼ inch of the edge. D: wires should not be placed there.
notes.explanation: Wires closer than ¼ inch to an edge need a grommet, and bundles are clamped at each bulkhead hole.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Protection Against Chafing”, PDF page 215
notes.evidence: Cable clamps should be used to support wire bundles at each hole through a bulkhead. [Figure 4-95] If wires come closer than ¼ inch to the edge of the hole, a suitable grommet is used in the hole.

notes.front: What is the closest any wire may be routed to a plumbing line, and may it be supported from a flammable-fluid line?
notes.back: ½ inch; never supported from a line carrying flammable fluid or oxygen.
notes.explanation: Between 2 inches and ½ inch, back-to-back clamps give rigid separation but not support.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Routing Precautions”, PDF page 216
notes.evidence: No wire should be routed so that it is located nearer than ½ inch to a plumbing line, nor should a wire or wire bundle be supported from a plumbing line that carries flammable fluids or oxygen.

notes.front: What minimum clearance should wiring keep from control cables?
notes.back: At least 3 inches; otherwise fit mechanical guards.
notes.explanation: The guards prevent contact between the wiring and the moving cables.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Routing Precautions”, PDF page 216
notes.evidence: Wiring should be routed to maintain a minimum clearance of at least 3 inches from control cables. If this cannot be accomplished, mechanical guards should be installed to prevent contact between wiring and control cables.

notes.front: A new harness must run beside an engine fuel line for a short distance. Which installation is acceptable?
notes.choices:
A) Wires clamped to the fuel line for support
B) Wires below the line, 1 inch away
C) Wires ¼ inch from the line
D) Wires above the line, at least ½ inch away, with both clamped to the same structure
notes.back: D) Wires above the line, at least ½ inch away, with both clamped to the same structure
notes.choicesExplained: A: wires must never be supported from a flammable-fluid line. B: wires should be level with or above the line. C: no wire may be nearer than ½ inch.
notes.explanation: Keep wires level with or above the line, never nearer than ½ inch, and never supported from it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Routing Precautions”, PDF page 216
notes.evidence: No wire should be routed so that it is located nearer than ½ inch to a plumbing line, nor should a wire or wire bundle be supported from a plumbing line that carries flammable fluids or oxygen.

notes.front: Where should the mounting screw of a cable clamp be relative to the wire bundle?
notes.back: Above the bundle.
notes.explanation: Clamps are installed at the proper mounting angle, ideally backed against structure.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Installation of Cable Clamps”, PDF page 216
notes.evidence: Cable clamps should be installed with regard to the proper mounting angle. [Figure 4-99] The mounting screw should be above the wire bundle.

notes.front: A harness runs through a junction box and then along structure with supports 18 inches apart. How should it be secured?
notes.choices:
A) Tied inside the junction box
B) Laced only inside the junction box, and tied between the supports
C) Left untied between the supports
D) Laced very tightly throughout so it cannot move
notes.back: B) Laced only inside the junction box, and tied between the supports
notes.choicesExplained: A: bundles in enclosures should be laced only. C: bundles are tied where supports are more than 12 inches apart. D: cord must not cut into or deform the insulation.
notes.explanation: Enclosures take lacing only, and ties are needed where supports exceed 12 inches.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Tying”, PDF page 218
notes.evidence: All wire groups or bundles should be tied where supports are more than 12 inches apart.

notes.front: With which knot does single-cord lacing start?
notes.back: A clove hitch with an extra loop, at the thick end of the bundle.
notes.explanation: Double-cord lacing instead starts with a bowline-on-a-bight.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Single-Cord Lacing”, PDF page 217
notes.evidence: The lacing procedure is started at the thick end of the wire group or bundle with a knot consisting of a clove hitch with an extra loop.

notes.front: Why must aluminium wire be stripped with extreme care?
notes.back: Its strands break very easily once nicked.
notes.explanation: Stripping tools must be adjusted carefully to avoid nicking or cutting strands.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Stripping Wire & Cable”, PDF page 220
notes.evidence: Aluminum wire must be stripped using extreme care, since individual strands break very easily after being nicked.

notes.front: Where should splicing of electrical cable be avoided entirely?
notes.back: In locations subject to extreme vibration; splicing is kept to a minimum everywhere.
notes.explanation: Splices in bundles must be where they can be inspected, and staggered so the bundle does not swell.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Solderless Terminals & Splices”, PDF page 220
notes.evidence: Splicing of electrical cable should be kept to a minimum and avoided entirely in locations subject to extreme vibrations.

notes.front: What terminal lugs may terminate aluminium wire?
notes.back: Only aluminium terminal lugs.
notes.explanation: Their barrels hold a petrolatum-zinc compound that grinds off the oxide film during crimping.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Aluminum Wire Terminals”, PDF page 222
notes.evidence: Only aluminum terminal lugs are used to terminate aluminum wires.

notes.front: A mechanic must fit a terminal on a No. 18 copper wire going to a terminal block. Which is the usual approach?
notes.choices:
A) An aluminium terminal lug
B) A soldered splice
C) Twisting the wire round the stud
D) A solderless preinsulated copper terminal lug, crimped with a ratcheting hand tool
notes.back: D) A solderless preinsulated copper terminal lug, crimped with a ratcheting hand tool
notes.choicesExplained: A: aluminium lugs are for aluminium wire. B: solder splices are brittle; terminals are crimped. C: wires are terminated with lugs for secure connection.
notes.explanation: Copper wires are terminated with solderless, preinsulated straight copper terminal lugs.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Copper Wire Terminals”, PDF page 221
notes.evidence: Copper wires are terminated with solderless, preinsulated straight copper terminal lugs.

notes.front: A broken No. 16 copper wire in a bundle, away from vibration, is repaired with a preinsulated permanent splice. What must the crimping include?
notes.choices:
A) Two crimping operations, one at each end of the splice
B) One crimp in the middle of the splice
C) Soldering after crimping
D) A petrolatum-zinc compound
notes.back: A) Two crimping operations, one at each end of the splice
notes.choicesExplained: B: each end needs its own crimp. C: the crimp alone makes this splice. D: that is for aluminium terminals.
notes.explanation: The crimping follows terminal lug practice but is done once for each end.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Splicing Copper Wires Using Preinsulated Wires”, PDF page 222
notes.evidence: The crimping procedures are the same as those used for terminal lugs, except that the crimping operation must be done twice, one for each end of the splice.

notes.front: May damaged aluminium wire be temporarily spliced?
notes.back: No; emergency splice repairs apply to copper wire only.
notes.explanation: Emergency repairs are temporary and must be replaced with permanent repairs as soon as possible.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Emergency Splicing Repairs”, PDF page 222
notes.evidence: These repairs are applicable to copper wire. Damaged aluminum wire must not be temporarily spliced. These repairs are for temporary emergency use only and should be replaced as soon as possible with permanent repairs.

notes.front: Where must no washer be placed when connecting terminal lugs on a stud?
notes.back: In the current path between two aluminium lugs or two copper lugs.
notes.explanation: Lugs are also locked against movement in the direction of loosening.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Connecting Terminal Lugs to Terminal Blocks”, PDF page 223
notes.evidence: Do not place any washer in the current path between two aluminum terminal lugs or between two copper terminal lugs.

notes.front: What is grounding?
notes.back: Electrically connecting a conducting object to the primary structure for return of current.
notes.explanation: Primary structure means the main frame, fuselage or wing structure.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Bonding & Grounding”, PDF page 224
notes.evidence: Grounding is the electrical connecting of a conducting object to the primary structure for return of current. Primary structure is the main frame, fuselage, or wing structure of the aircraft.

notes.front: A new avionics box has a ground lead to be attached. Which attachment follows the general procedures?
notes.choices:
A) To primary structure, on a smooth clean surface, secure against vibration
B) To a painted panel without removing the paint
C) Soldered to a tubular member
D) Daisy-chained through another box's ground
notes.back: A) To primary structure, on a smooth clean surface, secure against vibration
notes.choicesExplained: B: nonconducting finishes must be removed for a low-resistance joint. C: solder for bonding jumpers should be avoided; tubes use clamps. D: parts are bonded individually if possible.
notes.explanation: The procedures call for primary structure, clean surfaces and connections that vibration cannot loosen.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “General Bonding & Grounding Procedures”, PDF page 224
notes.evidence: Install bonding or grounding connections against smooth, clean surfaces.

notes.front: What is the maximum resistance of each bonding jumper connection?
notes.explanation: Jumpers are kept as short as practicable and must not hinder movable parts such as control surfaces.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Bonding & Grounding”, PDF page 224
notes.evidence: Bonding jumpers should be kept as short as practicable, and installed so that the resistance of each connection does not exceed 0.003 ohm.

notes.front: A mechanic fabricates a bonding jumper for an engine mount. The joint measures 0.010 ohm through a painted surface. What should be done?
notes.choices:
A) Remove the paint at the contact area, remake the joint and refinish it afterwards
B) Lengthen the jumper to reduce resistance
C) Solder the jumper in place
D) Accept it, as anything under 0.1 ohm is fine
notes.back: A) Remove the paint at the contact area, remake the joint and refinish it afterwards
notes.choicesExplained: B: jumpers are kept as short as practicable. C: solder for bonding jumpers should be avoided. D: each connection must not exceed 0.003 ohm.
notes.explanation: Paint is a nonconducting finish; removing it gives the low-resistance joint the limit requires.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Bonding & Grounding”, PDF page 224
notes.evidence: Bonding jumpers should be kept as short as practicable, and installed so that the resistance of each connection does not exceed 0.003 ohm.

notes.front: When replacing a connector, which half gets the socket-type insert?
notes.back: The half that stays live ("hot") after disconnection.
notes.explanation: The stated aim is to prevent unintentional grounding.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Connectors”, PDF page 226
notes.evidence: When replacing connector assemblies, the socket-type insert should be used on the half that is “ live” or “hot” after the connector is disconnected to prevent unintentional grounding.

notes.front: What is a class K connector?
notes.back: A fireproof steel connector for areas where current must not be interrupted even in continuous open flame.
notes.explanation: Its wires are crimped to the contacts, and it is normally longer than other classes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Types of Connectors”, PDF page 227
notes.evidence: Class K—a fireproof connector used in areas where it is vital that the electric current is not interrupted, even though the connector may be exposed to continuous open flame.

notes.front: A connector for a fire-detection circuit must keep working on an engine firewall exposed to flame. Which class fits?
notes.choices:
A) Class K
B) Class A
C) Class C
D) Class D
notes.back: A) Class K
notes.choicesExplained: B: it is a general-purpose solid back shell connector. C: it is a pressurised connector for bulkheads of pressurised equipment. D: it resists moisture and vibration, not continuous flame.
notes.explanation: Class K is the fireproof steel connector for circuits that must not be interrupted in flame.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Types of Connectors”, PDF page 227
notes.evidence: Class K—a fireproof connector used in areas where it is vital that the electric current is not interrupted, even though the connector may be exposed to continuous open flame.

notes.front: How far may connector pliers tighten a coupling ring beyond finger tight?
notes.back: One-sixteenth to one-eighth turn, only when there is too little room for a good finger grip.
notes.explanation: Pliers stand in for fingers only where there is no room to grip, so the extra turn is kept small; the handbook forbids forcing a plug home or hammering it in.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Installation of Connectors”, PDF page 228
notes.evidence: Never use force to mate connectors to receptacles. Do not hammer a plug into its receptacle and never use a torque wrench or pliers to lock coupling rings.

notes.front: How much larger than the bundle should a conduit's inner diameter be?
notes.back: About 25 percent larger than the maximum bundle diameter.
notes.explanation: The margin allows for ease of maintenance and future circuit expansion.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Conduit”, PDF page 228
notes.evidence: specifying the conduit inner diameter about 25 percent larger than the maximum diameter of the conductor bundle.

notes.front: Before adding electrical load, what must be checked?
notes.back: That previous maximum load plus added load does not exceed the ratings of existing wires, cables and protection devices.
notes.explanation: The total load must stay within the rated limits of the power-supply system.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Electrical Load Limits”, PDF page 229
notes.evidence: Before any aircraft electrical load is increased, the associated wires, cables, and circuit-protection devices, such as fuses or circuit breakers, should be checked to determine that the new electrical load—previous maximum load plus added load—does not exceed the rated limits

notes.front: An owner of a small aircraft with a 60-ampere generator wants extra equipment but no placards or load monitor. What total continuous load keeps the battery charging in flight?
notes.choices:
A) 60 amperes
B) 30 amperes
C) 72 amperes
D) About 48 amperes
notes.back: D) About 48 amperes
notes.choicesExplained: A: using the full rating leaves no assurance of battery charging. B: the guidance is about 80 percent, not 50. C: that exceeds the generator's rating.
notes.explanation: About 80 percent of rated output: 0.8 × 60 = 48 amperes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Controlling or Monitoring the Electrical Load”, PDF page 229
notes.evidence: the total continuous connected electrical load may be held to approximately 80 percent of the total rated generator output capacity.

notes.front: When should a circuit breaker or fuse open relative to its conductor's behaviour?
notes.back: Before the conductor emits smoke.
notes.explanation: So the device's time/current characteristic must fall below that of the conductor.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Circuit Protection Devices”, PDF page 229
notes.evidence: The circuit breaker or fuse should open the circuit before the conductor emits smoke. To accomplish this, the time/current characteristic of the protection device must fall below that of the associated conductor.

notes.front: An engine accessory circuit is being added. Which protection meets the handbook's guidance?
notes.choices:
A) An automatic reset breaker at the accessory
B) A trip-free breaker near the source bus that opens before the wire would smoke
C) A breaker rated well above the wire's own capacity
D) No protection, as the wire runs from the generator
notes.back: B) A trip-free breaker near the source bus that opens before the wire would smoke
notes.choicesExplained: A: automatic reset breakers should not be used in aircraft. C: the device must open before the conductor emits smoke. D: added load circuits must be protected.
notes.explanation: Protection sits close to the bus, trips free and has a time/current curve below the wire's.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Circuit Protection Devices”, PDF page 230
notes.evidence: All resettable circuit breakers should open the circuit in which they are installed, regardless of the position of the operating control when an overload or circuit fault exists. Such circuit breakers are referred to as trip-free.

notes.front: Why must a switch for incandescent lamps be derated?
notes.back: Lamps can draw an initial current 15 times their continuous current, which can burn or weld the contacts.
notes.explanation: The switch's stamped rating is for continuous current with contacts closed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Switches”, PDF page 230
notes.evidence: High rush-in circuits—circuits containing incandescent lamps can draw an initial current that is 15 times greater than the continuous current. Contact burning or welding may occur when the switch is closed.

notes.front: A switch stamped with a nominal rating is chosen for a DC motor circuit. What should the mechanic do?
notes.choices:
A) Derate it, as motors draw several times rated current at start and arc on opening
B) Use it at its stamped rating
C) Use a larger switch only for lamp circuits
D) Fit an automatic reset breaker instead
notes.back: A) Derate it, as motors draw several times rated current at start and arc on opening
notes.choicesExplained: B: the stamped figure is a continuous rating that motor circuits exceed. C: motor and inductive circuits need derating too. D: those are not to be used for aircraft protection.
notes.explanation: The stamped rating applies to continuous closed-contact current; motors exceed it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Switches”, PDF page 230
notes.evidence: Motors—direct current motors draw several times their rated current during starting, and magnetic energy stored in their armature and field coils is released when the control switch is opened.

notes.front: What do aircraft wiring diagrams typically specify?
notes.back: Wire size and terminal type, and each component's part and serial number.
notes.explanation: This is why they are often used to troubleshoot electrical malfunctions.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Wiring Diagrams”, PDF page 480
notes.evidence: Electrical wiring diagrams are included in most aircraft service manuals and specify information, such as the size of the wire and type of terminals to be used for a particular application.

notes.front: An engine's alternator field circuit has an intermittent fault. Which document best helps trace wire sizes, terminals and components?
notes.choices:
A) The type certificate data sheet
B) The oil grade chart
C) A block diagram only
D) The aircraft wiring diagram in the service manual
notes.back: D) The aircraft wiring diagram in the service manual
notes.choicesExplained: A: it does not detail individual wires and terminals. B: it has nothing to do with electrical circuits. C: blocks lump several components together.
notes.explanation: Wiring diagrams identify wire, terminals and components and are often used to troubleshoot.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “Wiring Diagrams”, PDF page 480
notes.evidence: Wiring diagrams are often used for troubleshooting electrical malfunctions.

notes.front: Which risk element in the certification standards' engine electrical task concerns cockpit warnings?
notes.back: Actions in response to a warning or caution annunciator light.
notes.explanation: The standards expect an applicant to identify, assess and mitigate the risks associated with it.
notes.source: Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-1), “III.F Engine Electrical Systems, risk management”, PDF page 55
notes.evidence: AM.III.F.R2 Actions in response to a warning or caution annunciator light.

notes.front: How do series and shunt wound generators differ in response to rising load?
notes.back: Series: voltage rises. Shunt: voltage falls.
notes.explanation: In a series machine the load current also magnetises the field; in a shunt machine the field sits across the output and load current passes only through the armature.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Types of DC Generators”, PDF page 171
notes.evidence: In a shunt generator, any increase in load causes a decrease in the output voltage, and any decrease in load causes an increase output voltage.

notes.front: How does aluminium wire compare with copper?
notes.back: Aluminium has about 60 percent of copper's conductivity but is lighter; copper is more ductile, stronger and easily soldered.
notes.explanation: Its light weight makes long spans possible, so it is used extensively despite lower conductivity.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Factors Affecting Selection of Conductor Material”, PDF page 209
notes.evidence: Although aluminum has only about 60 percent of the conductivity of copper, it is used extensively. Its light weight makes possible long spans

notes.front: How does tying differ from lacing?
notes.back: Tying uses separate pieces of cord at intervals; lacing uses one continuous cord forming loops.
notes.explanation: Both secure bundles for ease of installation, maintenance and inspection.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Lacing & Tying Wire Bundles”, PDF page 217
notes.evidence: Tying is the securing together of a group or bundle of wires by individual pieces of cord tied around the group or bundle at regular intervals.

notes.front: How does the output of a DC alternator differ from that of an AC alternator?
notes.back: A DC alternator rectifies its three-phase output to DC; an AC alternator sends three-phase AC to the buses unrectified.
notes.explanation: Both make three-phase AC internally; only the DC type turns it into ripple DC with diodes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B, 2023), “AC Alternators”, PDF page 456
notes.evidence: This wave pattern is similar to those produced internally by a DC alternator; however, in this case, the AC alternator does not rectify the voltage
